differences.aspect: Fit to the brief's learning mechanic
differences.design_x: The checkpoint signs directly label the next planet with its name plus a fact (options step: "พุธ: ใกล้ดวงอาทิตย์ที่สุด" etc.; build plan: "Use exactly 8 ordered checkpoints with these short Thai labels"). Players follow named targets, so the sequence is given rather than discovered.
differences.design_y: Each checkpoint gives a short clue about the next planet "without printing that next planet's name in the clue" (prototype decisions; build plan), so students must recall/apply knowledge to find the next planet — a stronger match to the brief's "discovery" feeling, at some risk of confusion.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype decisions: "มี 8 จุดตรวจ... จุดละข้อเท็จจริงสั้นหนึ่งข้อ" (8 checkpoints, one short fact each). Design Y prototype decisions: "ใช้คำใบ้สั้นเรื่องลักษณะเด่นหรือตำแหน่งของดวงถัดไป โดยไม่เขียนชื่อเฉลยไว้บนป้าย" (short clue about the next planet without revealing its name).

differences.aspect: Accuracy constraint (ข้อมูลต้องถูกต้อง)
differences.design_x: Gives eight concrete, correct planet facts at the options step and repeats them verbatim in the build plan labels; the start card states distances are not to scale.
differences.design_y: States the not-to-scale disclaimer as a decision and a rule, but never writes out the actual clue text, so correctness of the delivered content cannot be verified from the session.
differences.evidence: Design X options step lists all 8 facts (e.g., "เสาร์: มีวงแหวนที่เห็นได้ชัด"). Design Y build plan only instructs "a short, scientifically correct clue about the next planet" without the text itself.

differences.aspect: Real-space safety for first-time VR players
differences.design_x: Build plan: route segments at least 1.2 m wide, gameplay at least 0.6 m from the floor edge, planets placed beside never on the route, no void floor "เพราะผู้เล่นไม่เคยใช้วีอาร์" (because players have never used VR), rules say walk at normal speed and do not run.
differences.design_y: Prototype decisions and build plan: few static red hazards, walking gaps at least 1.2 m wide, route and props at least 0.6 m inside the boundary, "โดยไม่เร่งวิ่ง" (without rushing), morning lighting chosen for visibility of the real floor.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype decisions: "ไม่ใช้พื้นหลุมลึกเพราะผู้เล่นไม่เคยใช้วีอาร์". Design Y prototype decisions: "ใช้วงแดงนิ่งจำนวนน้อย กระจายให้มีช่องเดินหลบกว้างอย่างน้อย 1.2 เมตร".

differences.aspect: Spatial specificity and buildability of the layout
differences.design_x: The sketch and build plan give normalized coordinates for all 8 planet stops plus the start and finish portal (e.g., Sun (0.16,0.82), Neptune (0.17,0.22), portal (0.09,0.50)), with stops "approximately 1.5–3 m apart" — a builder can lay this out directly.
differences.design_y: The sketch collapses planets into three grouped zones (e.g., "ดาวพุธ ดาวศุกร์ โลก และดาวอังคาร" as one zone at (0.53,0.31)), so per-planet placement is undefined; the build plan describes the spiral only qualitatively.
differences.evidence: Design X build plan lists nine normalized positions; Design Y prototype sketch has only 3 story zones covering 8 planets.

differences.design_x: Option 1's zigzag route, two asteroid patches between Mars and Jupiter, and bleacher-side finish all carry through the prototype (storyboard climax, flow at 1:45, sketch danger zone) into the build plan unchanged.
differences.design_y: The option promises a "วงเวียนแบบเกลียวกว้างจากดวงอาทิตย์ตรงกลาง" (wide spiral from the Sun at the centre) and the prototype decisions repeat this, but the sketch path starts at (0.5,0.5) yet places the Mars–Jupiter hazard at (0.28,0.39) before Jupiter/Saturn at (0.28,0.59), and the build plan gives no coordinates to resolve whether the geometry actually spirals outward in order.
differences.evidence: Design Y options step route field vs. prototype sketch zone positions; Design X option route field "ซิกแซกจากดวงอาทิตย์ไปเนปจูน แล้วโค้งไปประตูจบฝั่งอัฒจันทร์" matches the sketch path and build plan exactly.

differences.design_x: The finish portal is explicitly placed "ฝั่งอัฒจันทร์" (on the bleacher side) at (0.09,0.50) and the asteroid climax "must face the bleachers"; the option's spectator_view mentions cheering, calling the next planet, and a team score screen.
differences.design_y: The build plan also asks for the Mars–Jupiter crossing and portal to face the bleachers, and the sketch includes an audience zone at (0.5,0.93), but the portal at (0.82,0.43) is on a different side of the sketch from the audience zone, leaving the sightline promise less grounded.
differences.evidence: Design X sketch goal zone name: "เนปจูนและประตูจบใกล้อัฒจันทร์" (Neptune and finish portal near the bleachers). Design Y sketch: audience zone at y=0.93, goal at (0.82,0.43).

differences.aspect: Lighting fit to a morning gym with windows
differences.design_x: Chooses "night" lighting with a deep-navy floor in both the option and build plan; it argues morning window light keeps the real room visible, but a dark space floor plus night mood works against the naturally bright room it must blend with.
differences.design_y: Chooses "morning" lighting and vivid accents "เพื่อให้อ่านง่ายท่ามกลางแสงเช้าจากหน้าต่าง" (for readability amid morning window light), explicitly avoiding reliance on intense glow — better matched to the venue's actual conditions.
differences.evidence: Design X option lighting: "night"; Design Y prototype decisions: "ใช้แสงแบบเช้าและสีสดเพื่อให้เห็นชัดในโรงยิม" and build plan: "avoid reliance on intense glow".

differences.design_x: Test questions include a direct learning measure: whether students can order all eight planet cards correctly after playing, compared with before playing.
differences.design_y: Test questions cover onboarding speed, clue readability, crowding, and completion rate, but none checks whether the solar-system order was actually learned.
differences.evidence: Design X prototype test_questions: "นักเรียนสามารถเรียงการ์ดดาวเคราะห์ทั้งแปด...ได้ถูกต้องหรือไม่ และดีขึ้นเมื่อเทียบกับก่อนเล่นหรือไม่"; Design Y test_questions have no equivalent item.

improvements: Design X should switch from night to morning-appropriate lighting (or justify the dark floor against window glare) and could adopt Design Y's clue-without-the-name mechanic to make discovery active rather than labelled.

Design Y should give per-planet coordinates in the sketch/build plan instead of grouped zones, write out the actual clue text so scientific accuracy can be verified, reconcile the spiral geometry with the bleacher-side portal placement, and add a post-play ordering assessment like Design X's.
summary: Both sessions converge on the same recommended concept — a four-player walk through the eight planets in order with an asteroid-belt hazard between Mars and Jupiter and a finish portal near the bleachers — and both carry it through prototype and build plans with matching scoring, timing, and safety margins. They differ in execution quality on different axes: Design X is more spatially specific (per-planet normalized coordinates), more internally consistent (zigzag route identical across all three steps), includes a real learning assessment question, and grounds the spectator sightline concretely, but it hands players the planet names directly (weaker discovery) and picks night lighting for a morning gym. Design Y has the stronger learning mechanic (clues that do not reveal the next planet's name), morning-appropriate lighting, and an explicit audience zone, but its sketch collapses eight planets into three grouped zones, its spiral geometry is not verifiably consistent with the bleacher-side finish, and it never writes the actual clue text needed to satisfy the accuracy constraint. These strengths and weaknesses roughly balance out.
why: Design X wins on specificity, cross-step consistency, spectator grounding, and learning assessment; Design Y wins on the discovery mechanic, lighting fit, and explicit audience zoning. Neither set of advantages clearly outweighs the other for this brief: Design X's weaknesses (labels that give away the answers, night lighting) are experiential, while Design Y's weaknesses (grouped zones, unwritten clue content, unresolved geometry) are executional but fixable at build time. With both sessions recommending and detailing essentially the same game with identical scoring, timing, and safety numbers, a tie is the honest verdict.
x_weaknesses: Checkpoint labels name each planet outright (build plan: 8 labels like "พุธ: ใกล้ดวงอาทิตย์ที่สุด"), so players follow signs rather than discover the order — weaker fit to the "discovery" feeling.
Lighting is set to "night" with a deep-navy floor in both the option and build plan, a questionable match for a morning gym with windows where the real room stays visible.

The prototype flow ends meaningful play at 3:50 with the last 10 seconds unspecified, and the 4-minute budget for 8 stops plus reading is asserted rather than stress-tested (buildability self-score of 4 at the options step).
y_weaknesses: The sketch groups eight planets into three story zones (e.g., one zone for Mercury–Mars at (0.53,0.31)), so the build plan lacks per-planet positions a builder could directly use.

The promised spiral from a central Sun is not verifiable against the sketch, and the portal (0.82,0.43) sits on a different side from the audience zone (0.5,0.93), leaving the spectator sightline claim weakly supported.

The actual clue text is never written anywhere in the session, so the brief's hard constraint that information must be correct cannot be checked, and no test question verifies that students learned the planet order.
